title: Towards the Characterization of Logical Errors in Distributed Lattice Surgery
authors: Nitish Kumar Chandra, Reza Nejabati, Eneet Kaur
abstract: Distributed quantum computing offers a scalable alternative to monolithic quantum processors by networking smaller quantum modules through shared entangled pairs. A central challenge in this setting is that inter-module quantum operations are typically noisier than intra-module local gates, which introduces additional noise into the system. In this work, we analyze distributed lattice surgery under heterogeneous noise conditions, focusing in particular on the merge operation as one of its fundamental subroutines. Specifically, we discuss the XX merge operation between two rotated surface-code patches hosted on two different quantum processors. We characterize logical errors in the resulting H-shaped spacetime diagram and estimate thresholds using a minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoder. We use a phenomenological noise model and derive distinct bulk and seam error rates to approximate a circuit-level noise model that includes contributions from local CNOT gates, noisy entangled pairs, idle errors, and readout errors. Our results provide practical insights into selecting the optimal surface-code distance, establishing target local-gate fidelities, and determining the tolerable entangled-pair fidelity required for logical operations in a distributed architecture.
summary: This paper analyzes how logical errors accumulate when performing lattice surgery across physically separated quantum modules. It models the merge operation using a detailed noise framework incorporating imperfections in shared entangled links. The results offer crucial, quantitative guidelines for designing fault-tolerant distributed quantum computers.
main_problem: The primary challenge is characterizing logical errors that accumulate during distributed quantum computation, specifically focusing on the merge operation in lattice surgery.
main_result: The work derives practical insights by providing quantitative estimates for required local-gate fidelities and tolerable entangled-pair fidelities necessary for fault-tolerant operations in a distributed architecture.
method: The analysis employs Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) decoding on an H-shaped spacetime diagram to estimate logical error rates under a phenomenological noise model.
model_or_system: The system is based on distributed quantum computing using smaller modules networked by shared entangled pairs, implementing the planar surface code via lattice surgery techniques.
key_observables: Logical Z errors in the XX merge operation; logical error rates ($\mathfrak{q}_{	ext{seam}}$); and operational thresholds.
important_parameters: Surface-code distance ($d$); Bell-pair noise scaling factor ($k$); local CNOT gate fidelities ($\epsilon_{cx}, \epsilon_m$).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a phenomenological noise model that explicitly accounts for contributions from imperfect Bell pairs, local gates, idling, and readout errors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the rotated surface code structure, entanglement-assisted nonlocal CNOT gates, the lattice surgery circuit for logical CNOTs, and the H-shaped spacetime diagram detailing the merge operation history.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the distributed setting to analyzing the core merge operation using syndrome measurements, developing a comprehensive noise model incorporating non-local errors, and finally deriving scaling laws for the resulting logical error rate.
why_interesting: It provides concrete quantitative metrics (thresholds and fidelity requirements) that bridge theoretical quantum error correction concepts with realistic hardware constraints imposed by networking multiple physical processors.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Entanglement-assisted nonlocal CNOT gate. A shared Bell pair is used to mediate the interaction between spatially separated control and target qubits, followed by local CNOTs, measurements, and classical feedforward for Pauli corrections.

Fig. 1. Rotated Surface Code for 𝑑= 5. The gray (𝑋-type) and white (𝑍-) squares represent the plaquettes (stabilizer generators) of the code. Data qubits are located at the vertices (grey circles). The vertical line indicates the logical X operator (𝑋𝐿), and the horizontal line indicates the logical Z operator (𝑍𝐿). The X and Z arches, indicated by arrows, represent the stabilizers at the boundary. We use red for 𝑋𝐿and Green 𝑍𝐿to represent the logical operators.

Fig. 3. Lattice surgery circuit for a logical CNOT gate. The control (|𝐶⟩) and target (|𝑇⟩) patches interact via an ancilla (|0⟩) using sequential joint parity measurements. The final byproduct Pauli corrections are dictated by the measurement outcomes 𝑎,𝑏, and 𝑐.
Fig. 4. Spacetime diagram of the H-shaped geometry for the merge operation in lattice surgery. The horizontal and vertical axes represent the qubits and syndrome extraction rounds, respectively.

Fig. 5. Ancilla mediated merge operation between two 𝑑= 5 rotated surface code patches. The central column of qubits, initialized in |0⟩, forms the bridge region used to couple the two patches during the merge. The dashed line marks the interface where joint stabilizers are measured, enabling a logical parity measurement between the two encoded qubits.
